name: Thiruvanchikulam Mahadeva Temple, Kodungallur
deity: Shiva as Mahadeva (Anjaikalathappar of the Tevaram), with the goddess Umadevi
period: The Paadal Petra Sthalam of Malai Nadu, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century)
summary: At Thiruvanchikulam near Kodungallur — the Thiruvanjaikalam of the Tevaram — stands Kerala's own Paadal Petra Sthalam, from where, tradition says, Sundarar rode to Kailash on a white elephant.

sections.history: Thiruvanchikulam lies about two kilometres south of Kodungallur in Thrissur district, close to the old Chera capital on the Periyar's mouth. Its Shiva temple is the Thiruvanjaikalam of the Tevaram and one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams — the Paadal Petra Sthalam of Malai Nadu, the one shrine of the Kerala country among them. Sundarar sang the Lord here, whom the Tamil hymns call Anjaikalathappar. The temple is bound up with Cheraman Perumal Nayanar, the Chera king who was Sundarar's devoted friend, and it is today protected as a monument by the Archaeological Survey of India.
sections.architecture: Unlike the Tevaram temples of the Tamil country, this is a Kerala temple in form: a sreekovil in the regional style, in which Shiva is worshipped as Sadashiva facing east, approached through a namaskara mandapam of sixteen pillars. The temple is known for its mural paintings, which depict scenes from the Puranas in the warm earth colours of the Kerala tradition, and for its images of Sundarar and Cheraman Perumal, the two friends who give the shrine its story.
sections.legends: Tradition says that at the end of his earthly life Sundarar was summoned to Kailash, and Shiva sent a white elephant to carry him there from Thiruvanjaikalam. Sundarar mounted it and rose into the sky; his friend Cheraman Perumal, unwilling to be left behind, followed on horseback. On the way, Sundarar sang his last pathigam, and the story goes that Varuna, lord of the sea, carried the hymn back to the Lord of Anjaikalam.
sections.festivals: The eight-day Maha Shivaratri festival in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (February–March) is the great event, with the Aanayottam elephant race drawing large crowds. On Swathi in Aadi (July–August), the images of Sundarar and Cheraman Perumal are brought in procession to remember their journey to Kailash; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: For pilgrims who have followed the Tevaram through the Tamil country, Thiruvanchikulam is a meeting of two worlds: Tamil hymns and Kerala ritual. Take time over the murals, stand before the Lord in the namaskara mandapam, and visit on Aadi Swathi to see the two friends carried in procession. The Kodungallur Bhagavathy temple is close by.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, following Kerala temple custom; hours change on festival days. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Traditional attire is expected. Men are often asked to remove upper garments and wear a mundu, and women to dress modestly in a saree or similar. Please confirm the current requirements at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is typically not permitted near the sanctum and may be restricted in the precincts. Please ask staff and follow their instructions, especially during festivals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 2 km south of Kodungallur town in Thrissur district, near Kottappuram on the road towards Ernakulam. Irinjalakuda, Thrissur and Ernakulam are the nearest railheads, and Cochin International Airport is roughly 30 km away by road.
